title: Pegasus Finance — LLM migration discovery: deployment fit & compatibility
summary: Initial discovery for migrating Pegasus Finance's conversational and summarization pipelines off a mixed stack (OpenAI + vLLM on-prem experiments). Primary concerns: eval parity, latency SLOs for trading alerts, data residency and KMS/HSM integration for private deployments, and cost predictability. Redwood AE+SE introduced hosted/dedicated/private options and proposed an eval sprint with benchmark plan.
action_items: Maya Chen | Send hosting comparison sheet (hosted vs dedicated vs private) | Due: 2026-07-06
Ravi Banerjee | Share draft benchmark script + sample prompts for Pegasus conversational flows | Due: 2026-07-07
Lena Ortiz | Provide representative prompt set and 3 weeks of latency histograms from current infra | Due: 2026-07-08
next_steps: Redwood to run 2-week eval: hosted test + dedicated baseline with sample prompts
Schedule technical deep-dive on private deployment requirements (Priya + Redwood infra lead) — proposed 2026-07-09
Exchange security questionnaire and SOC 2 + encryption docs via SSO link
meeting_header: Date: 2026-07-03 | Time: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Banerjee (Redwood SE), Olivia Park (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Pegasus Head of ML), Tom Hargreaves (Platform), Priya Singh (Security), Elliot Marsh (Product)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you blocking time. Quick roll call please.
[00:05] Lena Ortiz: Lena here, hi.
[00:06] Tom Hargreaves: Tom — platform eng.
[00:07] Priya Singh: Priya — security.
[00:09] Elliot Marsh: Elliot here.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Great. Ravi and Olivia from our infra team are here too — we'll mostly be listening for constraints and then riff on an eval plan. Rough agenda is current stack, main pain points, security/reqs, and then an outline of an eval. Sound good?
[00:25] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. To set context, we run a hybrid setup: production is primarily OpenAI for chat and summarization, and we have an on-prem vLLM layer for latency-critical alerts. We're experimenting with TGI for nightly batch reranks. The problem is cost volatility and maintainability.
[00:40] Ravi Banerjee: When you say latency-critical alerts, what SLAs do you need?
[00:43] Lena Ortiz: For trading alerts we need 150ms p95 end-to-end — includes network and model. For other customer-facing chat, 500ms p95 is acceptable.
[00:52] Tom Hargreaves: Also, the vLLM ops are a nightmare: memory fragmentation, kv cache thrash — we sometimes see spikes where throughput tanks.
[01:02] Olivia Park: When you mention KV cache thrash, are you running pinned KV across requests or recreating per session?
[01:07] Tom Hargreaves: It's per session right now, trying to avoid cross-tenant leakage in our current approach.
[01:13] Priya Singh: From security angle, we need KMS integration (HSM preferred), SSO with SAML, RBAC and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Also strict data residency for EU PII.
[01:25] Maya Chen: All very common asks. Redwood supports KMS integrations and can pull audit logs; our Private deployment runs in a customer VPC and supports HSM via customer KMS. We can also do Dedicated with VPC peering for stronger isolation.
[01:40] Elliot Marsh: On the regimen of eval parity — we want to make sure switching providers doesn't degrade hallucination rates on our summarization prompts. How do you measure that?
[01:50] Ravi Banerjee: Good question. For eval parity we typically run side-by-side generation on a representative prompt set and compare precision/recall-ish metrics — BLEU/ROUGE aren't perfect for semantics so we also use human raters on samples and automated hallucination detectors. We'll propose an eval harness.
[02:05] Lena Ortiz: Can you run the tests against our proprietary prompts in hosted mode? We are nervous about sending our prompts to hosted endpoints unless there's an NDA and data controls.
[02:14] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we can sign an NDA. For hosted tests we can set up ephemeral projects where logs are not retained or we can scrub inputs. Alternatively, Dedicated gives you the safest path for sensitive prompts during eval.
[02:27] Tom Hargreaves: Cost is huge for us. OpenAI spend has spiky months. How does Redwood bill — token-based still? Any way to get predictability?
[02:36] Maya Chen: Hosted is usage-based (per-token and features). Dedicated is committed capacity — you buy reserved GPU pools which smooths unit costs and gives throughput SLAs. Private is licensed and predictable but has platform fees. We can run a cost model once we see your token distribution.
[02:50] Priya Singh: For Private/on-prem we need to know about patching and upgrade windows. We cannot have automatic upgrades that break inference behavior in prod windows.
[03:00] Olivia Park: Understood. Our Private deployment supports controlled rollouts and freeze windows; upgrades are orchestrated with canary policies and you can pin model versions.
[03:10] Lena Ortiz: What about vLLM and TGI compatibility? We currently have some models converted to vLLM formats; will those artifacts work with Redwood runtime or do we need to re-quantize?
[03:20] Ravi Banerjee: The runtime accepts standard model formats. For vLLM-specific optimizations we profile and may recommend quantization variants. If you have a custom kernel or patched runtime, we'll need to validate. In practice most PyTorch/Transformers checkpoints load fine.
[03:35] Tom Hargreaves: We run some models quantized to 4-bit; does Redwood support quantized inference on Dedicated/Private?
[03:40] Ravi Banerjee: Yes — we support several quantization profiles. Dedicated can run int8/4-bit optimized kernels; private deployments can use local toolchains if you need specific quant libs.
[03:48] Elliot Marsh: Streaming and function calling are important to our UX — does Redwood's hosted API support streaming?
[03:53] Maya Chen: Hosted supports streaming responses, function/tool-calling patterns, and structured outputs. We also expose SDKs for web sockets if needed.
[04:02] Lena Ortiz: Anything we should be worried about if we try to run a mixed test: hosted for bulk and dedicated for latency?
[04:08] Olivia Park: Mixed routing is a standard policy. We route by latency and cost preferences; fallback policies are configurable if capacity is limited. One caveat: prefix cache miss rates can differ between environments, so we may see some inconsistency that we account for in the eval.
[04:23] Priya Singh: On encryption, encryption at rest is required and keys in our KMS only. How does Redwood handle that for hosted?
[04:31] Maya Chen: For hosted we offer customer-managed keys (BYOK) in certain plans; for Private it's your KMS. We will share the security spec doc after this call.
[04:40] Tom Hargreaves: Can we run perf tests that mimic 150ms p95? If not, we can't justify ripping out vLLM yet.
[04:47] Ravi Banerjee: We can. Proposed approach: run representative prompt set over your sample traffic in three phases — hosted baseline, dedicated baseline with reserved capacity tuned for your p95, and private smoke test if needed. We'll instrument end-to-end latency including network hops.
[05:03] Lena Ortiz: How long does a dedicated baseline setup take?
[05:06] Maya Chen: For a small pilot it can be as quick as 48-72 hours to provision reserved capacity once contracts are in place; hosted is immediate. Private takes longer due to VPC and KMS setup — usually 2–4 weeks depending on your infra team bandwidth.
[05:20] Elliot Marsh: On monitoring, do you provide token-level cost and latency breakouts? We need to attribute spend to product features.
[05:27] Olivia Park: Yes — Redwood Console gives per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost, tracing hooks and error analysis. You can export to your data lake or SIEM.
[05:36] Tom Hargreaves: For the eval, can you share a sample benchmark spreadsheet?
[05:39] Maya Chen: We'll share a benchmark template with fields for prompts, expected outputs, latency, token counts, and a slot for human rating.
[05:46] Lena Ortiz: We have compliance checks — SOC 2 and ISO are baseline. Also need a vendor security questionnaire answered.
[05:54] Maya Chen: We'll send SOC 2 reports and a completed vendor questionnaire copy. Priya, any specific red flags we should watch for?
[06:00] Priya Singh: HSM integration, audit log retention, and confirmation that data in logs can be redacted. Also legal wants clarity on data retention of request/response for hosted evals.
[06:10] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll propose ephemeral logs for the hosted eval and a contract addendum if needed.
[06:16] Elliot Marsh: Can you run a small smoke test on hosted with scrambled prompts before we share production prompts?
[06:20] Ravi Banerjee: Yes. We recommend a three-step eval: (1) smoke with scrambled prompts in hosted, (2) hosted with scrubbed prompts, (3) dedicated baseline using reserved capacity.
[06:31] Lena Ortiz: Timeline wise we'd like results within two weeks to present to execs.
[06:34] Maya Chen: That's doable — we'll propose a sprint that starts next week and delivers a results dashboard with comparisons.
[06:40] Tom Hargreaves: Any known regressions when moving from OpenAI to open-source backends? We saw subtle behavior differences in naming entities and factuality.
[06:49] Ravi Banerjee: Differences are common due to model weights and tokenizers. We surface a delta report that breaks down where outputs diverge, and we tune prompts and system messages as part of the eval. Sometimes a tiny prompt rewrite resolves alignment issues.
[07:02] Lena Ortiz: Great. On commercial, what commitment would we need for a dedicated pool that meets 150ms p95?
[07:09] Maya Chen: We can give a sizing estimate after we see your traffic. Typical approach is a short char-reverse: run load test to observe concurrency and tokens/sec and then propose a committed GPU capacity with burst policies.
[07:22] Elliot Marsh: What about SLAs for uptime and latency?
[07:25] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; private is contract-defined with options for on-prem support windows.
[07:33] Priya Singh: Make sure SLA penalties and maintenance windows are explicit in the contract.
[07:38] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll include those clauses.
[07:42] Tom Hargreaves: Any performance gotchas with quantized models on your runtime vs our current vLLM setup?
[07:49] Ravi Banerjee: Quantization behavior is model-dependent. Our runtime includes kernel selection and compilation heuristics; sometimes a different quant profile yields better latency/quality tradeoffs. We'll include that in the eval matrix.
[07:59] Lena Ortiz: Ok let's recap real quick — can someone list the mutually agreed next actions?
[08:04] Maya Chen: I'll list — (1) Send hosting comparison and benchmark template (Maya) (2) Share benchmark script and sample prompts (Ravi) (3) Pegasus to provide prompt set and latency histograms (Lena) (4) Schedule security deep-dive (Priya + Redwood infra) (5) Draft eval schedule aiming for two-week sprint.
[08:20] Lena Ortiz: Matches our notes.
[08:22] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[08:24] Priya Singh: Please include SOC 2 report and a copy of the security questionnaire answers.
[08:28] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[08:33] Elliot Marsh: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:34] [meeting ends]

Notes: Links to be shared after call — hosted-vs-dedicated-comparison.pdf, eval-benchmark-template.csv, redwood-security-spec.pdf. Some transcription artifacts: 'kv cache' was transcribed sometimes as 'K V cash'; speaker labels had occasional 'Speaker 1' in backup.
